entries.d4460386883f7d1ddd79e1063feafe0f2df242eb: <div sID="gen2123" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="34" osisID="Exod.34" sID="Exod.34"/> <div eID="gen2123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2124" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2125" type="x-p"/> God having in the foregoing chapter intimated to Moses his reconciliation to Israel, here gives proofs of it, proceeding to settle his covenant and communion with them. Four instances of the return of his favour we have in this chapter:—I. The orders he gives to Moses to come up to the mount, the next morning, and bring two tables of stone with him, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.1-Exod.34.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. His meeting him there, and the proclamation of his name, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.5-Exod.34.9">ver. 5-9</reference>. III. The instructions he gave him there, and his converse with him for forty days together, without intermission, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.10-Exod.34.28">ver. 10-28</reference>. IV. The honour he put upon him when he sent him down with his face shining, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.29-Exod.34.35">ver. 29-35</reference>. In all this God dealt with Moses as a public person, and mediator between him and Israel, and a type of the great Mediator.
entries.26b2aabd58f735072bfc9433b8b8d6138bd298d0: <div eID="gen2125" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2124" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Proclamation of Himself. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen2126" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first: and I will write upon <hi type="italic">these</hi> tables the words that were in the first tables, which thou brakest. <hi type="super">2</hi> And be ready in the morning, and come up in the morning unto Mount Sinai, and present thyself there to me in the top of the mount. <hi type="super">3</hi> And no man shall come up with thee, neither let any man be seen throughout all the mount; neither let the flocks nor herds feed before that mount. 4 And he hewed two tables of stone like unto the first; and Moses rose up early in the morning, and went up unto Mount Sinai, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had commanded him, and took in his hand the two tables of stone. <div eID="gen2126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2127" type="x-p"/> The treaty that was on foot between God and Israel being broken off abruptly, by their worshipping the golden calf, when peace was made all must be begun anew, not where they left off, but from the beginning. Thus backsliders must <hi type="italic">repent, and do their first works,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.2.5">Rev. ii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen2127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2128" type="x-p"/> I. Moses must prepare for the renewing of the tables, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.1">v. 1</reference>. Before, God himself provided the tables, and wrote on them; now, Moses must <hi type="italic">hew out the tables,</hi> and God would only write upon them. Thus, in the first writing of the law upon the heart of man in innocency, both the tables and the writing were the work of God; but when those were broken and defaced by sin, and the divine law was to be preserved in the scriptures, God therein made use of the ministry of man, and Moses first. But the prophets and apostles did only hew the tables, as it were; the writing was God's still, for <hi type="italic">all scripture is given by inspiration of God.</hi> Observe, When God was reconciled to them, he ordered the tables to be renewed, and wrote his law in them, which plainly intimates to us, 1. That even under the gospel of peace and reconciliation by Christ (of which the intercession of Moses was typical) the moral law should continue to bind believers. Though Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law, yet not from the command of it, but still we are <hi type="italic">under the law to Christ;</hi> when our Saviour, in his sermon on the mount, expounded the moral law, and vindicated it from the corrupt glosses with which the scribes and Pharisees had broken it (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.19">Matt. v. 19</reference>), he did in effect renew the tables, and make them like the first, that is, reduce the law to its primitive sense and intention. 2. That the best evidence of the pardon of sin and peace with God is the writing of the law in the heart. The first token God gave of his reconciliation to Israel was the renewing of the tables of the law; thus the first article of the new covenant is, <hi type="italic">I will write my law in their heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.10">Heb. viii. 10</reference>), and it follows (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.12">v. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">for I will be merciful to their unrighteousness.</hi> 3. That, if we would have God to write the law in our hearts, we must prepare our hearts for the reception of it. The heart of stone must be hewn by conviction and humiliation for sin (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.5">Hos. vi. 5</reference>), the <hi type="italic">superfluity of naughtiness</hi> must be taken off (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.21">James i. 21</reference>), the heart made smooth, and laboured with, that the word may have a place in it. Moses did accordingly hew out the <hi type="italic">tables of stone,</hi> or slate, for they were so slight and thin that Moses carried them both in his hand; and, for their dimensions, they must have been somewhat less, and perhaps not much, than the ark in which they were deposited, which was a yard and quarter long, and three quarters broad. It should seem there was nothing particularly curious in the framing of them, for there was no great time taken; Moses had them ready presently, to take up with him, next morning. They were to receive their beauty, not from the art of man, but from the finger of God. <div eID="gen2128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2129" type="x-p"/> II. Moses must attend again on the top of Mount Sinai, and present himself to God there, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.2">v. 2</reference>. Though the absence of Moses, and his continuance so long on the mount, had lately occasioned their making the golden calf, yet God did not therefore alter his measures, but he shall come up and tarry as long as he had done, to try whether they had learned to wait. To strike an awe upon the people, they are directed to keep their distance, none must come up with him, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.3">v. 3</reference>. They had said (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.1">ch. xxxii. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">We know not what has become of him,</hi> and God will not let them know. Moses, accordingly, <hi type="italic">rose up early</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.4">v. 4</reference>) to go to the place appointed, to show how forward he was to present himself before God and loth to lose time. It is good to be early at our devotions. The morning is perhaps as good a friend to the graces as it is to the muses.
entries.fb0c757ffb6c168f323ce749db9908f4fdc81669: <div eID="gen2129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2130" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> descended in the cloud, and stood with him there, and proclaimed the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">6</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> passed by before him, and proclaimed, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, <hi type="super">7</hi> Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear <hi type="italic">the guilty;</hi> visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth <hi type="italic">generation.</hi> 8 And Moses made haste, and bowed his head toward the earth, and worshipped. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he said, If now I have found grace in thy sight, O Lord, let my Lord, I pray thee, go among us; for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a stiffnecked people; and pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for thine inheritance. <div eID="gen2130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2131" type="x-p"/> No sooner had Moses got to the top of the mount than God gave him the meeting (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord descended,</hi> by some sensible token of his presence, and manifestation of his glory. His descending bespeaks his condescension; he humbles himself to take cognizance of those that humble themselves to walk with him. <reference osisRef="Ps.113.6">Ps. cxiii. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">Lord, what is man, that he should be thus visited?</hi> He descended <hi type="italic">in the cloud,</hi> probably that pillar of cloud which had hitherto gone before Israel, and had the day before met Moses at the door of the tabernacle. This cloud was to strike an awe upon Moses, that the familiarity he was admitted to might not breed contempt. The disciples <hi type="italic">feared, when they entered the cloud.</hi> His making a cloud his pavilion intimated that, though he made known much of himself, yet there was much more concealed. Now observe, <div eID="gen2131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2132" type="x-p"/> I. How God proclaimed his name (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.6-Exod.34.7">v. 6, 7</reference>): he did it <hi type="italic">in transitu—as he passed by him.</hi> Fixed views of God are reserved for the future state; the best we have in this world are transient. God now was performing what he had promised Moses, the day before, that his glory should pass by, <reference osisRef="Exod.33.22">ch. xxxiii. 22</reference>. He <hi type="italic">proclaimed the name of the Lord,</hi> by which he would make himself known. He had made himself known to Moses in the glory of his self-existence and self-sufficiency when he proclaimed that name, <hi type="italic">I am that I am;</hi> now he makes himself known in the glory of his grace, and goodness, and all-sufficiency to us. Now that God is about to publish a second edition of the law he prefaces it with this proclamation; for it is God's grace or goodness that gives the law, especially the remedial law. The pardon of Israel's sin in worshipping the calf was now to pass the seals; and God, by this declaration, would let them know that he pardoned <hi type="italic">ex mero motu—merely out of his own good pleasure,</hi> not for their merits' sake, but from his own inclination to forgive. The proclaiming of it denotes the universal extent of God's mercy. He is not only good to Israel, but good to all; let all take notice of it. He that hath an ear, let him hear, and know, and believe, <div eID="gen2132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2133" type="x-p"/> 1. That the God with whom we have to do is a great God. He is Jehovah, the Lord, who has his being of himself, and is the fountain of all being, <hi type="italic">Jehovah-El, the Lord, the strong God,</hi> a God of almighty power himself, and the original of all power. This is prefixed before the display of his mercy, to teach us to think and to speak even of God's grace and goodness with great seriousness and a holy awe, and to encourage us to depend upon these mercies; they are not the mercies of a man, that is frail and feeble, false and fickle, but the mercies of the Lord, the Lord God; therefore sure mercies, and sovereign mercies, mercies that may be trusted, but not tempted. <div eID="gen2133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2134" type="x-p"/> 2. That he is a good God. His greatness and goodness illustrate and set off each other. That the terror of his greatness may not make us afraid, we are told how good he is; and, that we may not presume upon his goodness, we are told how great he is. Many words are here heaped up, to acquaint us with, and convince us of, God's goodness, and to show how much his goodness is both his glory and his delight, yet without any tautology. (1.) He is <hi type="italic">merciful.</hi> This bespeaks his tender compassion, like that of a father to his children. This is put first, because it is the first wheel in all the instances of God's good-will to fallen man, whose misery makes him an object of pity, <reference osisRef="Judg.10.16">Judg. x. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Isa. lxiii. 9</reference>. Let us not then have either hard thoughts of God or hard hearts towards our brethren. (2.) He is <hi type="italic">gracious.</hi> This bespeaks both freeness and kindness; it intimates not only that he has a compassion to his creatures, but a complacency in them and in doing good to them, and this of his own good-will, and not for the sake of any thing in them. His mercy is grace, free grace; this teaches us to be not only pitiful, but courteous, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.8">1 Pet. iii. 8</reference>. (3.) He is <hi type="italic">long-suffering.</hi> This is a branch of God's goodness which the wickedness of sinners gives occasion for; that of Israel had done so: they had tried his patience, and experienced it. He is long-suffering, that is, he is slow to anger, and delays the execution of his justice; he waits to be gracious, and lengthens out the offers of his mercy. (4.) He is <hi type="italic">abundant in goodness and truth.</hi> This bespeaks plentiful goodness, goodness abounding above our deserts, above our conception and expression. The springs of mercy are always full, the streams of mercy always flowing; there is mercy enough in God, enough for all, enough for each, enough for ever. It bespeaks promised goodness, goodness and truth put together, goodness engaged by promise, and his faithfulness pledged for the security of it. He not only does good, but by his promise he raises our expectation of it, and even binds himself to show mercy. (5.) He keepeth <hi type="italic">mercy for thousands.</hi> This denotes, [1.] Mercy extended to thousands of persons. When he gives to some, still he keeps for others, and is never exhausted; he has mercy enough for all the thousands of Israel, when they shall <hi type="italic">multiply as the sand.</hi> [2.] Mercy entailed upon thousands of generations, even those upon whom the ends of the world have come; nay, the line of it is drawn parallel with that of eternity itself. (6.) He <hi type="italic">for giveth iniquity, transgression, and sin.</hi> Pardoning mercy is specified, because in this divine grace is most magnified, and because in this divine grace is most magnified, and because it is this which opens the door to all other gifts of his divine grace, and because of this he had lately given a very pregnant proof. He forgives offences of all sorts—<hi type="italic">iniquity, transgression, and sin,</hi> multiplies his pardons; and with him is <hi type="italic">plenteous redemption.</hi> <div eID="gen2134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2135" type="x-p"/> 3. That he is a just and holy God. For, (1.) <hi type="italic">He will by no means clear the guilty.</hi> Some read it so as to express a mitigation of wrath, even when he does punish: <hi type="italic">When he empties, he will not make quite desolate;</hi> that is, "He does not proceed to the greatest extremity, till there be no remedy." As we read it, we must expound it that he will by no means connive at the guilty, as if he took no notice of their sin. Or, he will not clear the impenitently guilty, that go on still in their trespasses: he will not clear the guilty without some satisfaction to his justice, and necessary vindications of the honour of his government. (2.) <hi type="italic">He visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children.</hi> He may justly do it, for all souls are his, and there is a malignity in sin that taints the blood. He sometimes will do it, especially for the punishment of idolaters. Thus he shows his hatred to sin, and displeasure against it; yet he <hi type="italic">keepeth not his anger for ever,</hi> but visits to the third and fourth generation only, while he <hi type="italic">keepeth his mercy for thousands.</hi> Well, this is God's name for ever, and this is his memorial unto all generations. <div eID="gen2135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2136" type="x-p"/> II. How Moses received this declaration which God made of himself, and of his grace and mercy. It should seem as if Moses accepted this as a sufficient answer to his request that God would <hi type="italic">show him his glory;</hi> for we read not that he went into the cleft of the rock, whence to gain a sight of God's back parts. Perhaps this satisfied him, and he desired no more; as we read not that Thomas did <hi type="italic">thrust his hand into Christ's side,</hi> though Christ invited him to do it. God having thus proclaimed his name, Moses says, "It is enough, I expect no more till I come to heaven;" at least he did not think fit to relate what he saw. Now we are here told, <div eID="gen2136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2137" type="x-p"/> 1. What impression it made upon him: <hi type="italic">Moses made haste, and bowed his head,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.34.8">v. 8</reference>. Thus he expressed, (1.) His humble reverence and adoration of God's glory, giving him <hi type="italic">the honour due to that name</hi> he had thus proclaimed. Even the goodness of God must be looked upon by us with a profound veneration and holy awe. (2.) His joy in this discovery which God had made of himself, and his thankfulness for it. We have reason gratefully to acknowledge God's goodness to us, not only in the real instances of it, but in the declarations he has made of it by his word; not only that he is, and will be, gracious to us, but that he is pleased to let us know it. (3.) His holy submission to the will of God, made known in this declaration, subscribing to his justice as well as mercy, and putting himself and his people Israel under the government and direction of such a God as Jehovah had now proclaimed himself to be. Let this God be our God for ever and ever. <div eID="gen2137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2138" type="x-p"/> 2. What improvement he made of it. He immediately grounded a prayer upon it (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.9">v. 9</reference>); and a more earnest affectionate prayer it is, (1.) For the presence of God with his people Israel in the wilderness: "<hi type="italic">I pray thee, go among us,</hi> for thy presence is all in all to our safety and success." (2.) For pardon of sin: "<hi type="italic">O pardon our iniquity and our sin,</hi> else we cannot expect thee to go among us." And, (3.) For the privileges of a peculiar people: "Take us for <hi type="italic">thy inheritance,</hi> which thou wilt have a particular eye to, and concern for, and delight in." These things God had already promised, and given Moses assurances of, and yet he prays for them, not as doubting the sincerity of God's grants, but as one solicitous for the ratification of them. God's promises are intended, not to supersede, but to direct and encourage, prayer. Those who have some good hopes, through grace, that their sins are pardoned, must yet continue to pray for pardon, for the renewing of their pardon, and the clearing of it more and more to their souls. The more we see of God's goodness the more ashamed we should be of our own sins, and the more earnest for an interest in it. God had said, in the close of the proclamation, that he would <hi type="italic">visit the iniquity upon the children;</hi> and Moses here deprecates that. "Lord, do not only pardon it to them, but to their children, and let our covenant-relation to thee be entailed upon our posterity, as an inheritance." Thus Moses, like a man of a truly public spirit, intercedes even for the children that should be born. But it is a strange plea he urges: <hi type="italic">For it is a stiff-necked people.</hi> God had given this as a reason why he would not go along with them, <reference osisRef="Exod.33.3">ch. xxxiii. 3</reference>. "Yea," says Moses, "the rather go along with us; for the worse they are the more need they have of thy presence and grace to make them better." Moses sees them so stiff-necked that, for his part, he has neither patience nor power enough to deal with them. "Therefore, Lord, do thou go among us, else they will never be kept in awe. Thou wilt spare, and bear with them, for thou art <hi type="italic">God, and not man,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Hos.11.9">Hos. xi. 9</reference>.
entries.986c828db68c6c7b3cdf10c1a00fead7dece0240: <div eID="gen2138" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">A Caution Against Idolatry. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen2139" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And he said, Behold, I make a covenant: before all thy people I will do marvels, such as have not been done in all the earth, nor in any nation: and all the people among which thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> shall see the work of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a terrible thing that I will do with thee. <hi type="super">11</hi> Observe thou that which I command thee this day: behold, I drive out before thee the Amorite, and the Canaanite, and the Hittite, and the Perizzite, and the Hivite, and the Jebusite. <hi type="super">12</hi> Take heed to thyself, lest thou make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land whither thou goest, lest it be for a snare in the midst of thee: <hi type="super">13</hi> But ye shall destroy their altars, break their images, and cut down their groves: <hi type="super">14</hi> For thou shalt worship no other god: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , whose name <hi type="italic">is</hi> Jealous, <hi type="italic">is</hi> a jealous God: <hi type="super">15</hi> Lest thou make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and they go a whoring after their gods, and do sacrifice unto their gods, and <hi type="italic">one</hi> call thee, and thou eat of his sacrifice; <hi type="super">16</hi> And thou take of their daughters unto thy sons, and their daughters go a whoring after their gods, and make thy sons go a whoring after their gods. <hi type="super">17</hi> Thou shalt make thee no molten gods. <div eID="gen2139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2140" type="x-p"/> Reconciliation being made, a covenant of friendship is here settled between God and Israel. The traitors are not only pardoned, but preferred and made favourites again. Well may the assurances of this be ushered in with a <hi type="italic">behold,</hi> a word commanding attention and admiration: <hi type="italic">Behold, I make a covenant.</hi> When the covenant was broken, it was Israel that broke it; now that it comes to be renewed, it is God that makes it. If there be quarrels, we must bear all the blame; if there be peace, God must have all the glory. Here is, <div eID="gen2140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2141" type="x-p"/> I. God's part of this covenant, what he would do for them, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.10-Exod.34.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. 1. In general: <hi type="italic">Before all thy people, I will do marvels.</hi> Note, Covenant-blessings are marvellous things (<reference osisRef="Ps.98.1">Ps. xcviii. 1</reference>), marvels in the kingdom of grace; those mentioned here were marvels in the kingdom of nature, the drying up of Jordan, the standing still of the sun, &c. Marvels indeed, for they were without precedent, <hi type="italic">such as have not been done in all the earth.</hi> They were the joy of Israel, and the confirmation of their faith: <hi type="italic">Thy people shall see,</hi> and own <hi type="italic">the work of the Lord.</hi> And they were the terror of their enemies: <hi type="italic">It is a terrible thing that I will do.</hi> Nay, even God's own people should see them with astonishment. 2. In particular: <hi type="italic">I drive out before thee the Amorite.</hi> God, as King of nations, plucks up some, to plant others, as it pleases him; as King of saints, he made room for the vine he brought out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.8-Ps.80.9">Ps. lxxx. 8, 9</reference>. Kingdoms are sacrificed to Israel's interests, <reference osisRef="Isa.43.3-Isa.43.4">Isa. xliii. 3, 4</reference>. <div eID="gen2141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2142" type="x-p"/> II. Their part of the covenant: <hi type="italic">Observe that which I command thee.</hi> We cannot expect the benefit of the promises unless we make conscience of the precepts. <div eID="gen2142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2143" type="x-p"/> 1. The two great precepts are, (1.) <hi type="italic">Thou shalt worship no other gods</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.14">v. 14</reference>), not give divine honour to any creature, or any name whatsoever, the creature of fancy. A good reason is annexed. It is at thy peril if thou do: <hi type="italic">For the Lord, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God,</hi> as tender in the matters of his worship as the husband is of the honour of the marriage-bed. Jealousy is called the <hi type="italic">rage of a man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.34">Prov. vi. 34</reference>), but it is <hi type="italic">God's holy and just displeasure.</hi> Those cannot worship God aright who do not worship him alone. (2.) "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt make thee no molten god</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.17">v. 17</reference>); thou shalt not worship the true God by images." This was the sin they had lately fallen into, which therefore they are particularly cautioned against. <div eID="gen2143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2144" type="x-p"/> 2. Fences are here erected about these two precepts by two others: (1.) That they might not be tempted to worship other gods, they must not join in affinity or friendship with those that did (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Take heed to thyself,</hi> for thou art upon thy good behaviour. It is a sin that thou art prone to and that will easily beset thee, and therefore be very cautious, and carefully abstain from all appearances of it and advances towards it. <hi type="italic">Make no covenant with the inhabitants of the land.</hi>" If God, in kindness to them, drove out the Canaanites, they ought, in duty to God, not to harbour them. What could be insisted on more reasonable than this? If God make war with the Canaanites, let not Israel make peace with them. If God take care that the Canaanites be not their lords, let them take care that they be not their snares. It was for their civil interest to complete the conquest of the land; so much does God consult our benefit in the laws he gives us. They must particularly take heed of intermarrying with them, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.15-Exod.34.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. If they espoused their children, they would be in danger of espousing their gods; such is the corruption of nature that the bad are much more likely to debauch the good than the good to reform the bad. The way of sin is downhill: those that are in league with idolaters will come by degrees to be in love with idolatry; and those that are prevailed upon to eat of the idolatrous sacrifice will come at length to offer it. <hi type="italic">Obsta principiis—Nip the mischief in the bud.</hi> (2.) That they might not be tempted to make molten gods, they must utterly destroy those they found and all that belong to them, the altars and groves (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.13">v. 13</reference>), lest, if these were left standing, they should be brought, in process of time, either to use them or to take pattern by them, or to abate in their detestation and dread of idolatry. The relics of idolatry ought to be abolished as affronts to the holy God and a great reproach to human nature. Let it never be said that men who pretend to reason were ever guilty of such absurdities as to make gods of their own and worship them.
entries.c19c70e8afd8fd0dd06977904fb4d0f8adf8a092: <div eID="gen2144" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Solemn Feasts Appointed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen2145" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> The feast of unleavened bread shalt thou keep. Seven days thou shalt eat unleavened bread, as I commanded thee, in the time of the month Abib: for in the month Abib thou camest out from Egypt. <hi type="super">19</hi> All that openeth the matrix <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine; and every firstling among thy cattle, <hi type="italic">whether</hi> ox or sheep, <hi type="italic">that is male.</hi> <hi type="super">20</hi> But the firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb: and if thou redeem <hi type="italic">him</hi> not, then shalt thou break his neck. All the firstborn of thy sons thou shalt redeem. And none shall appear before me empty. <hi type="super">21</hi> Six days thou shalt work, but on the seventh day thou shalt rest: in earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest. <hi type="super">22</hi> And thou shalt observe the feast of weeks, of the firstfruits of wheat harvest, and the feast of ingathering at the year's end. <hi type="super">23</hi> Thrice in the year shall all your men children appear before the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , the God of Israel. <hi type="super">24</hi> For I will cast out the nations before thee, and enlarge thy borders: neither shall any man desire thy land, when thou shalt go up to appear before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God thrice in the year. <hi type="super">25</hi> Thou shalt not offer the blood of my sacrifice with leaven; neither shall the sacrifice of the feast of the passover be left unto the morning. <hi type="super">26</hi> The first of the firstfruits of thy land thou shalt bring unto the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God. Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Write thou these words: for after the tenor of these words I have made a covenant with thee and with Israel. <div eID="gen2145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2146" type="x-p"/> Here is a repetition of several appointments made before, especially relating to their solemn feasts. When they had made the calf, they proclaimed a feast in honour of it; now, that they might never do so again, they are here charged with the observance of the feasts which God had instituted. Note, Men need not be drawn from their religion by the temptation of mirth, for we serve a Master that has abundantly provided for the joy of his servants: serious godliness is a continual feast, and joy in God always. <div eID="gen2146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2147" type="x-p"/> I. Once a week they must rest (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.21">v. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">even in earing time, and in harvest,</hi> the most busy times of the year. All worldly business must give way to that holy rest; harvest-work will prosper the better for the religious observance of the sabbath-day in harvest-time. Hereby we must show that we prefer our communion with God, and our duty to him, before either the business or the joy of harvest. <div eID="gen2147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2148" type="x-p"/> II. Thrice a year they must feast (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.23">v. 23</reference>); they must then appear <hi type="italic">before the Lord, God, the God of Israel.</hi> In all our religious approaches to God, we must eye him as the Lord God, infinitely blessed, great, and glorious, that we may worship him with reverence and godly fear, as the God of Israel, a God in covenant with us, that we may be encouraged to trust in him, and to serve him cheerfully. We always are before God; but, in holy duties, we present ourselves before him, as servants to receive commands, as petitioners to sue for favours, and we have reason to do both with joy. But it might be suggested that, when all the males from every part of the country had gone up to worship in the place that God should choose, the country would be left exposed to the insults of their neighbours; and what would become of the poor women and children, and sick and aged, that were left at home? Trust God with them (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Neither shall any man desire thy land;</hi> not only they shall not invade it, but they shall not so much as think of invading it. Note, 1. All hearts are in God's hands, and under his check; he can lay a restraint, not only upon men's actions, but upon their desires. Canaan was a desirable land, and the neighbouring nations were greedy enough; and yet God says, "They shall not desire it." Let us check all sinful desires in our own hearts against God and his glory, and then trust him to check all sinful desires in the hearts of others against us and our interest. 2. The way of duty is the way of safety. If we serve God, he will preserve us; and those that venture for him shall never lose by him. While we are employed in God's work, and are attending upon him, we are taken under special protection, as noblemen and members of parliament are privileged from arrests. <div eID="gen2148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2149" type="x-p"/> III. The three feasts are here mentioned, with their appendages. 1. The passover, and the feast of unleavened bread, in remembrance of their deliverance out of Egypt; and to this is annexed the law of the redemption of the first-born, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.18-Exod.34.20">v. 18-20</reference>. This feast was instituted, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.13">ch. xii. 13</reference>, and urged again, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.15">ch. xxiii. 15</reference>. 2. The feast of weeks, that is, that of pentecost, seven weeks after the passover; and to this is annexed the law of the first-fruits. 3. The feast of in-gathering at the year's end, which was the feast of tabernacles (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.22">v. 22</reference>): of these also he had spoken before, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.16">ch. xxiii. 16</reference>. As to those laws repeated here (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.25-Exod.34.26">v. 25, 26</reference>), that against leaven relates to the passover, that of the first-fruits to the feast of pentecost, and therefore that against seething the kid in his mother's milk in all probability relates to the feast of in-gathering, at which God would not have them use that superstitious ceremony, which probably they had seen the Egyptians, or some other of the neighbouring nations, bless their harvests with. <div eID="gen2149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2150" type="x-p"/> IV. With these laws, here repeated, it is probable all that was said to him when he was before upon the mount was repeated likewise, and the model of the tabernacle shown him again, lest the ruffle and discomposure, which the golden calf had put him in to should have bereaved him of the ideas he had in mind of what he had seen and heard; also in token of a complete reconciliation, and to show that <hi type="italic">not one jot or tittle of the law should pass away,</hi> but that all should be carefully preserved by the great Mediator, who came not to destroy, but to fulfil, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.17-Matt.5.18">Matt. v. 17, 18</reference>. And in the close, 1. Moses is ordered to write these words (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.27">v. 27</reference>), that the people might be the better acquainted with them by a frequent perusal, and that they might be transmitted to the generations to come. We can never be enough thankful to God for the written word. 2. He is told that according to the tenour of these words God would make a covenant with Moses and Israel; not with Israel immediately, but with them in Moses a mediator. Thus the covenant of grace is made with believers through Christ, who is <hi type="italic">given for a covenant to the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.8">Isa. xlix. 8</reference>. And, as here the covenant was made according to the tenour of the command, so it is still; for we are by baptism brought into covenant, that we may be <hi type="italic">taught to observe all things whatsoever Christ has commanded us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.28.19-Matt.28.20">Matt. xxviii. 19, 20</reference>.
entries.6a05dc3889c8773b809c3bf92b6f0246d6d4f5d3: <div eID="gen2150" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Veil of Moses. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1491.)</title> <div sID="gen2151" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> And he was there with the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> forty days and forty nights; he did neither eat bread, nor drink water. And he wrote upon the tables the words of the covenant, the ten commandments. <hi type="super">29</hi> And it came to pass, when Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tables of testimony in Moses' hand, when he came down from the mount, that Moses wist not that the skin of his face shone while he talked with him. <hi type="super">30</hi> And when Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone; and they were afraid to come nigh him. <hi type="super">31</hi> And Moses called unto them; and Aaron and all the rulers of the congregation returned unto him: and Moses talked with them. <hi type="super">32</hi> And afterward all the children of Israel came nigh: and he gave them in commandment all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had spoken with him in mount Sinai. <hi type="super">33</hi> And <hi type="italic">till</hi> Moses had done speaking with them, he put a vail on his face. <hi type="super">34</hi> But when Moses went in before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to speak with him, he took the vail off, until he came out. And he came out, and spake unto the children of Israel <hi type="italic">that</hi> which he was commanded. <hi type="super">35</hi> And the children of Israel saw the face of Moses, that the skin of Moses' face shone: and Moses put the vail upon his face again, until he went in to speak with him. <div eID="gen2151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2152" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The continuance of Moses in the mount, where he was miraculously sustained, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.28">v. 28</reference>. He was there in very intimate communion with God, without interruption, forty days and forty nights, and did not think it long. When we are weary of an hour or two spent in attendance upon God and adoration of him, we should think how many days and nights Moses spent with him, and of the eternal day we hope to spend in praising him. During all this time Moses did neither eat nor drink. Though he had before been kept so long fasting, yet he did not, this second time, take up so many days' provision along with him, but believed that <hi type="italic">man lives not by bread alone,</hi> and encouraged himself with the experience he had of the truth of it. So long he continued without meat and drink (and probably without sleep too), for, 1. The power of God supported him, that he did not need it. He who made the body can nourish it without ordinary means, which he uses, but is not tied to. <hi type="italic">The life is more than meat.</hi> 2. His communion with God entertained him, so that he did not desire it. He had meat to eat which the world knew not of, for it was his meat and drink to hear the word of God and pray. The abundant satisfaction his soul had in the word of God and the visions of the Almighty made him forget the body and the pleasures of it. When God would treat his favourite Moses, it was not with meat and drink, but with his light, law, and love, with the knowledge of himself and his will; then man did indeed eat angels' food. See what we should value as the truest pleasure. <hi type="italic">The kingdom of God is not meat and drink,</hi> neither the abundance nor delicacy of food, but <hi type="italic">righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Ghost.</hi> As Moses, so Elijah and Christ, fasted forty days and forty nights. The more dead we are to the delights of sense the better prepared we are for the pleasures of heaven. <div eID="gen2152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2153" type="x-p"/> II. The coming down of Moses from the mount, greatly enriched and miraculously adorned. <div eID="gen2153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2154" type="x-p"/> 1. He came down enriched with the best treasure; for he brought in his hands the two tables of the law, written with the finger of God, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.28-Exod.34.29">v. 28, 29</reference>. It is a great favour to have the law given us; this favour was shown to Israel, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.19-Ps.147.20">Ps. cxlvii. 19, 20</reference>. It is a great honour to be employed in delivering God's law to others; this honour was done to Moses. <div eID="gen2154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2155" type="x-p"/> 2. He came down adorned with the best beauty; for the <hi type="italic">skin of his face shone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.34.29">v. 29</reference>. This time of his being in the mount he heard only what he had heard before, but he saw more of the glory of God, which having with open face beheld, he was in some measure <hi type="italic">changed into the same image from glory to glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2 Cor. iii. 18</reference>. The last time he came down from the mount with the glory of a magistrate, to frown upon and chastise Israel's idolatry; now with the glory of an angel, with tidings of peace and reconciliation. Then he came with a rod, now with the spirit of meekness. Now, <div eID="gen2155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2156" type="x-p"/> (1.) This may be looked upon, [1.] As a great honour done to Moses, that the people might never again question his mission nor think nor speak lightly of him. He carried his credentials in his very countenance, which, some think, retained, as long as he lived, some remainders of this glory, which perhaps contributed to the vigour of his old age; that eye could not wax dim which had seen God, nor that face become wrinkled which had shone with his glory. The Israelites could not look him in the face but they must there read his commission. Thus it was done to the man whom the King of kings did delight to honour. Yet, after this, they murmured against him; for the most sensible proofs will not of themselves conquer an obstinate infidelity. The shining of Moses's face was a great honour to him; yet that was no glory, in comparison with the glory which excelled. We read of our Lord Jesus, not only that <hi type="italic">his face shone</hi> as the sun, but his whole body also, for his <hi type="italic">raiment was white and glistering,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.29">Luke ix. 29</reference>. But, when he came down from the mount, he quite laid aside that glory, it being his will that we should <hi type="italic">walk by faith, not by sight.</hi> [2.] It was also a great favour to the people, and an encouragement to them, that God put this glory upon him, who was their intercessor, thereby giving them assurance that he was accepted, and they through him. Thus the advancement of Christ, our advocate with the Father, is the great support of our faith. [3.] It was the effect of his sight of God. Communion with God, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Makes the face to shine in true honour. Serious godliness puts a lustre upon a man's countenance, such as commands esteem and affection. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It should make the face to shine in universal holiness. When we have been in the mount with God, we should let our <hi type="italic">light shine before men,</hi> in humility, meekness, and all the instances of a heavenly conversation; thus must the <hi type="italic">beauty of the Lord our God be upon us,</hi> even the <hi type="italic">beauty of holiness,</hi> that all we converse with may <hi type="italic">take knowledge of us that we have been with Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.4.13">Acts iv. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen2156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2157" type="x-p"/> (2.) Concerning the shining of Moses's face observe here, [1.] Moses was not aware of it himself: <hi type="italic">He wist not that the skin of his face shone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.34.29">v. 29</reference>. Thus, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is the infelicity of some that, though their faces shine in true grace, yet they do not know it, to take the comfort of it. Their friends see much of God in them, but they themselves are ready to think they have no grace. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is the humility of others that, though their faces shine in eminent gifts and usefulness, yet they do not know it, to be puffed up with it. Whatever beauty God puts upon us, we should still be filled with a humble sense of our own unworthiness, and manifold infirmities, as will make us even overlook and forget that which makes our faces shine. [2.] Aaron and the children of Israel saw it, and <hi type="italic">were afraid,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.34.30">v. 30</reference>. The truth of it was attested by a multitude of witnesses, who were also conscious of the terror of it. It not only dazzled their eyes, but struck such an awe upon them as obliged them to retire. Probably they doubted whether it were a token of God's favour or of his displeasure; and, though it seemed most likely to be a good omen, yet, being conscious of guilt, they feared the worst, especially remembering the posture Moses found them in when he came last down from the mount. Holiness will command reverence; but the sense of sin makes men afraid of their friends, and even of that which really is a favour to them. [3.] Moses put a <hi type="italic">veil upon his face,</hi> when he perceived that it shone, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.33">v. 33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.35">35</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> This teaches us all a lesson of modesty and humility. We must be content to have our excellences obscured, and a veil drawn over them, not coveting to <hi type="italic">make a fair show in the flesh.</hi> Those that are truly desirous to be owned and accepted of God will likewise desire not to be taken notice of nor applauded by men. <hi type="italic">Qui bene latuit, bene vixit—There is a laudable concealment. Secondly,</hi> It teaches ministers to accommodate themselves to the capacities of people, and to preach to them as they are able to bear it. Let all that art and all that learning be veiled which tend to amusement rather than edification, and let the strong condescend to the infirmities of the weak. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> This veil signified the darkness of that dispensation. The ceremonial institutions had in them much of Christ, much of the grace of the gospel, but a veil was drawn over it, so that the children of Israel could not distinctly and <hi type="italic">stedfastly see those good things to come which the law had the shadow of.</hi> It was beauty veiled, gold in the mine, a pearl in the shell; but, thanks be to God, by the gospel life and immortality are brought to light, the veil is taken away from off the Old Testament; yet still it remains upon the hearts of those who shut their eyes against the light. Thus the apostle expounds this passage, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13-2Cor.3.15">2 Cor. iii. 13-15</reference>. [4.] When Moses <hi type="italic">went in before the Lord,</hi> to speak with him in the tabernacle of meeting, he <hi type="italic">put off the veil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.34.34">v. 34</reference>. Then there was no occasion for it, and, before God, every man does and must appear unveiled; for <hi type="italic">all things are naked and open before the eyes of him with whom we have to do,</hi> and it is folly for us to think of concealing or disguising any thing. Every veil must be thrown aside when we come to present ourselves unto the Lord. This signified also, as it is explained (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.16">2 Cor. iii. 16</reference>), that when a soul turns to the Lord the veil shall be taken away, and with open face it may behold his glory. And when we shall come before the Lord in heaven, to be there for ever speaking with him, the veil shall not only be taken off from the divine glory, but from our hearts and eyes, that we may see as we are seen, and know as we are known.  <chapter eID="Exod.34"/> <div eID="gen2157" type="x-p"/>

entries.35f5c9c5fddd03f5b8add40fa7df87a4b9b79d23: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv932"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 34</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Exod.34.1-Exod.34.35">Ex 34:1-35</reference>. The Tables Are Renewed.</title> <div sID="gen1295" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv932"/><hi type="bold">1. the like unto the first--</hi>God having been reconciled to repentant Israel, through the earnest intercession, the successful mediation of Moses, means were to be taken for the restoration of the broken covenant. Intimation was given, however, in a most intelligible and expressive manner, that the favor was to be restored with some memento of the rupture; for at the former time God Himself had provided the materials, as well as written upon them. Now, Moses was to prepare the stone tables, and God was only to retrace the characters originally inscribed for the use and guidance of the people. <div eID="gen1295" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d3deb781e2ad82e9740a1dc981065f1066d55fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv933"/><div sID="gen1296" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv933"/><hi type="bold">2. present thyself ... to me in the top of the mount--</hi>Not absolutely the highest peak; for as the cloud of the Shekinah usually abode on the summit, and yet (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.5">Ex 34:5</reference>) it "descended," the plain inference is that Moses was to station himself at a point not far distant, but still below the loftiest pinnacle. <div eID="gen1296" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f6bf7885123be167e8e3d5a9db0d075e733ed0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv934"/><div sID="gen1297" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv934"/><hi type="bold">3. no man shall come up with thee ... neither ... flocks nor herds--</hi>All these enactments were made in order that the law might be a second time renewed with the solemnity and sanctity that marked its first delivery. The whole transaction was ordered so as to impress the people with an awful sense of the holiness of God; and that it was a matter of no trifling moment to have subjected Him, so to speak, to the necessity of re-delivering the law of the ten commandments. <div eID="gen1297" type="x-p"/>
entries.4916b3738c328bdb9bc93db18d250078f37b5a3b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv935"/><div sID="gen1298" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv935"/><hi type="bold">4. Moses ... took in his hand the two tables of stone--</hi>As Moses had no attendant to divide the labor of carrying them, it is evident that they must have been light, and of no great dimensions--probably flat slabs of shale or slate, such as abound in the mountainous region of Horeb. An additional proof of their comparatively small size appears in the circumstance of their being deposited in the ark of the most holy place (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.10">Ex 25:10</reference>). <div eID="gen1298" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ed0931657bf169f2a463234fe3836ca7b195492: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv936"/><div sID="gen1299" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv936"/><hi type="bold">5. the Lord descended in the cloud--</hi>After graciously hovering over the tabernacle, it seems to have resumed its usual position on the summit of the mount. It was the shadow of God manifest to the outward senses; and, at the same time, of God manifest in the flesh. The emblem of a cloud seems to have been chosen to signify that, although He was pleased to make known much about himself, there was more veiled from mortal view. It was to check presumption and engender awe and give a humble sense of human attainments in divine knowledge, as now man sees, but darkly. <div eID="gen1299" type="x-p"/>
entries.04857202b2db552a8ed07a763d1733ce8a2574e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv937"/><div sID="gen1300" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv937"/><hi type="bold">6. the Lord passed by before him--</hi>in this remarkable scene, God performed what He had promised to Moses the day before.<div eID="gen1300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1301" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">proclaimed, The Lord ... merciful and gracious--</hi>At an earlier period He had announced Himself to Moses, in the glory of His self-existent and eternal majesty, as "I am" [Ex 3:14]; now He makes Himself known in the glory of His grace and goodness--attributes that were to be illustriously displayed in the future history and experience of the church. Being about to republish His law--the sin of the Israelites being forgiven and the deed of pardon about to be signed and sealed by renewing the terms of the former covenant--it was the most fitting time to proclaim the extent of the divine mercy which was to be displayed, not in the case of Israel only, but of all who offend. <div eID="gen1301" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea5293da9e7cdf1bb9da1485e50de0f404059c60: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv938"/><div sID="gen1302" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv938"/><hi type="bold">8-26. Moses bowed ... and worshipped--</hi>In the East, people bow the head to royalty, and are silent when it passes by, while in the West, they take off their hats and shout. <div eID="gen1302" type="x-p"/>
entries.8191343c2cf4a9234d6b41756766de8d78a99244: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv940"/><div sID="gen1304" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv940"/><hi type="bold">27-28. And the Lord said unto Moses, Write thou these words--</hi>that is, the ceremonial and judicial injunctions comprehended above (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.11-Exod.34.26">Ex 34:11-26</reference>); while the rewriting of the ten commandments on the newly prepared slabs was done by God Himself (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.10.1-Deut.10.4">De 10:1-4</reference>). <div eID="gen1304" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1d8533f7d510e85c253e77c6c0edd77ad51012a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv942"/><div sID="gen1306" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv942"/><hi type="bold">29. Moses wist not that the skin of his face shone while he talked with him--</hi>It was an intimation of the exalted presence into which he had been admitted and of the glory he had witnessed (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>); and in that view, it was a badge of his high office as the ambassador of God. No testimonial needed to be produced. He bore his credentials on his very face; and whether this extraordinary effulgence was a permanent or merely temporary distinction, it cannot be doubted that this reflected glory was given him as an honor before all the people. <div eID="gen1306" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0472fbeaf8654d55e77f8a512501d02616f3517: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv943"/><div sID="gen1307" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv943"/><hi type="bold">30. they were afraid to come nigh him--</hi>Their fear arose from a sense of guilt--the beaming radiance of his countenance made him appear to their awe-struck consciences a flaming minister of heaven. <div eID="gen1307" type="x-p"/>
entries.808cdfe42cfa4b4b437522ac36aba92ee56d6555: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv944"/><div sID="gen1308" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv944"/><hi type="bold">33. he put a veil on his face--</hi>That veil was with the greatest propriety removed when speaking with the Lord, for every one appears unveiled to the eye of Omniscience; but it was replaced on returning to the people--and this was emblematic of the dark and shadowy character of that dispensation (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13">2Co 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.14">14</reference>). <chapter eID="Exod.34"/>

entries.7aa526448e5b833b691e29c7a25680215165d00f: <div eID="gen4023" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen4024" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4025" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4025" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4024" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4026" type="x-p"/> Moses is commanded to hew two tables similar to the first, and bring them up to the mount, to get the covenant renewed, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.1-Exo.34.3">Exo 34:1-3</reference>. He prepares the tables and goes up to meet the Lord, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.4">Exo 34:4</reference>. The Lord descends, and proclaims his name Jehovah, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.5">Exo 34:5</reference>. What this name signifies, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.6">Exo 34:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.7">Exo 34:7</reference>. Moses worships and intercedes, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.8">Exo 34:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.9">Exo 34:9</reference>. The Lord promises to renew the covenant, work miracles among the people, and drive out the Canaanites, etc., <reference osisRef="Exo.34.10">Exo 34:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.11">Exo 34:11</reference>. No covenant to be made with the idolatrous nations, but their altars and images to be destroyed, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.12-Exo.34.15">Exo 34:12-15</reference>. No matrimonial alliances to be contracted with them, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.16">Exo 34:16</reference>. The Israelites must have no molten gods, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.17">Exo 34:17</reference>. The commandment of the feast of unleavened bread, and of the sanctification of the first-born, renewed, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.18-Exo.34.29">Exo 34:18-29</reference>; as also that of the Sabbath, and the three great annual feasts, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.21-Exo.34.23">Exo 34:21-23</reference>. The promise that the surrounding nations shall not invade their territories, while all the males were at Jerusalem celebrating the annual feasts, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.24">Exo 34:24</reference>. Directions concerning the passover, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.25">Exo 34:25</reference>; and the first-fruits, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.26">Exo 34:26</reference>. Moses is commanded to write all these words, as containing the covenant which God had now renewed with the Israelites, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.27">Exo 34:27</reference>. Moses, being forty days with God without eating or drinking, writes the words of the covenant; and the Lord writes the ten commandments upon the tables of stone, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.28">Exo 34:28</reference>. Moses descends with the tables; his face shines, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.29">Exo 34:29</reference>. Aaron and the people are afraid to approach him, because of his glorious appearance, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.30">Exo 34:30</reference>. Moses delivers to them the covenant and commandments of the Lord; and puts a veil over his face while he is speaking, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.31-Exo.34.33">Exo 34:31-33</reference>, but takes it off when he goes to minister before the Lord, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.34">Exo 34:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.35">Exo 34:35</reference>. <div eID="gen4026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4027" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen4027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4028" type="x-p"/> Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first - In <reference osisRef="Exo.32.16">Exo 32:16</reference> we are told that the two first tables were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God; but here Moses is commanded to provide tables of his own workmanship, and God promises to write on them the words which were on the first. That God wrote the first tables himself, see proved by different passages of Scripture at the end of Exodus 32 (<reference osisRef="Exo.32.35">Exo 32:35</reference> (note)). But here, in <reference osisRef="Exo.34.27">Exo 34:27</reference>, it seems as if Moses was commanded to write these words, and in <reference osisRef="Exo.34.28">Exo 34:28</reference> it is said, And he wrote upon the tables; but in <reference osisRef="Deu.10.1-Deu.10.4">Deu 10:1-4</reference> it is expressly said that God wrote the second tables as well as the first. <div eID="gen4028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4029" type="x-p"/> In order to reconcile these accounts let us suppose that the ten words, or ten commandments, were written on both tables by the hand of God himself, and that what Moses wrote, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.27">Exo 34:27</reference>, was a copy of these to be delivered to the people, while the tables themselves were laid up in the ark before the testimony, whither the people could not go to consult them, and therefore a copy was necessary for the use of the congregation; this copy, being taken off under the direction of God, was authenticated equally with the original, and the original itself was laid up as a record to which all succeeding copies might be continually referred, in order to prevent corruption. This supposition removes the apparent contradiction; and thus both God and Moses may be said to have written the covenant and the ten commandments: the former, the original; the latter, the copy. This supposition is rendered still more probable by <reference osisRef="Exo.34.27">Exo 34:27</reference> itself: "And the Lord said unto Moses, Write thou these words (that is, as I understand it, a copy of the words which God had already written); for After The Tenor (על פי al pi According To The Mouth) of these words I have made a covenant with thee and with Israel." Here the original writing is represented by an elegant prosopopoesia, or personification, as speaking and giving out from its own mouth a copy of itself. It may be supposed that this mode of interpretation is contradicted by <reference osisRef="Exo.34.28">Exo 34:28</reference> : And He wrote upon the tables the words of the covenant; but that the pronoun He refers to the Lord, and not to Moses, is sufficiently proved by the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Deu.10.1-Deu.10.4">Deu 10:1-4</reference> : At that time the Lord said unto me, Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first - and I will write on the tables the words that were in the first tables - and I hewed two tables of stone as at the first - And He wrote on the tables according to the first writing. This determines the business, and proves that God wrote the second as well as the first tables, and that the pronoun in <reference osisRef="Exo.34.28">Exo 34:28</reference> refers to the Lord, and not to Moses. By this mode of interpretation all contradiction is removed. Houbigant imagines that the difficulty may be removed by supposing that God wrote the ten commandments, and that Moses wrote the other parts of the covenant from <reference osisRef="Exo.34.11">Exo 34:11</reference> to <reference osisRef="Exo.34.26">Exo 34:26</reference>, and thus it might be said that both God and Moses wrote on the same tables. This is not an improbable case, and is left to the reader's consideration. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.34.27">Exo 34:27</reference>. <div eID="gen4029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4030" type="x-p"/> There still remains a controversy whether what are called the ten commandments were at all written on the first tables, those tables containing, according to some, only the terms of the covenant without the ten words, which are supposed to be added here for the first time. "The following is a general view of this subject. In Exodus 20 the ten commandments are given; and at the same time various political and ecclesiastical statutes, which are detailed in chapters 21, 22, and 23. To receive these, Moses had drawn near unto the thick darkness where God was, <reference osisRef="Exo.20.21">Exo 20:21</reference>, and having received them he came again with them to the people, according to their request before expressed, <reference osisRef="Exo.20.19">Exo 20:19</reference> : Speak thou with us - but let not the Lord speak with us, lest we die, for they had been terrified by the manner in which God had uttered the ten commandments; see <reference osisRef="Exo.20.18">Exo 20:18</reference>. After this Moses, with Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and the seventy elders, went up to the mountain; and on his return he announced all these laws unto the people, <reference osisRef="Exo.24.1-Exo.24.3">Exo 24:1-3</reference>, etc., and they promised obedience. Still there is no word of the tables of stone. Then he wrote all in a book, <reference osisRef="Exo.24.4">Exo 24:4</reference>, which was called the book of the covenant, <reference osisRef="Exo.24.7">Exo 24:7</reference>. After this there was a second going up of Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders, <reference osisRef="Exo.24.9">Exo 24:9</reference>, when that glorious discovery of God mentioned in <reference osisRef="Exo.24.10">Exo 24:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.24.11">Exo 24:11</reference> took place. After their coming down Moses is again commanded to go up; and God promises to give him tables of stone, containing a law and precepts, <reference osisRef="Exo.24.12">Exo 24:12</reference>. This is the first place these tables of stone are mentioned; and thus it appears that the ten commandments, and several other precepts, were given to and accepted by the people, and the covenant sacrifice offered, <reference osisRef="Exo.24.5">Exo 24:5</reference>, before the tables of stone were either written or mentioned." It is very likely that the commandments, laws, etc., were first published by the Lord in the hearing of the people; repeated afterwards by Moses; and the ten words or commandments, containing the sum and substance of the whole, afterwards written on the first tables of stone, to be kept for a record in the ark. These being broken, as is related <reference osisRef="Exo.32.19">Exo 32:19</reference>, Moses is commanded to hew out two tables like to the first, and bring them up to the mountain, that God might write upon them what he had written on the former, <reference osisRef="Exo.34.1">Exo 34:1</reference>. And that this was accordingly done, see the preceding part of this note.
entries.cca88571caabec0d85ed41793bce5a4c7f806c4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen4030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4031" type="x-p"/> And the Lord passed by - and proclaimed, The Lord, etc. - It would be much better to read this verse thus: "And the Lord passed by before him, and proclaimed Jehovah," that is, showed Moses fully what was implied in this august name. Moses had requested God to show him his glory, (see the preceding chapter, <reference osisRef="Exo.33.18">Exo 33:18</reference> (note)), and God promised to proclaim or fully declare the name Jehovah, (<reference osisRef="Exo.33.19">Exo 33:19</reference>); by which proclamation or interpretation Moses should see how God would "be gracious to whom he would be gracious," and how he would "be merciful to those to whom he would show mercy. Here therefore God fulfils that promise by proclaiming this name. It has long been a question, what is the meaning of the word יהוה Jehovah, Yehovah, Yehue, Yehveh, or Yeve, Jeue, Jao, Iao, Jhueh, and Jove; for it has been as variously pronounced as it has been differently interpreted. Some have maintained that it is utterly inexplicable; these of course have offered no mode of interpretation. Others say that it implies the essence of the Divine nature. Others, that it expresses the doctrine of the Trinity connected with the incarnation; the letter י yod standing for the Father, ה he for the Son, and ו vau (the connecting particle) for the Holy Spirit: and they add that the ה he being repeated in the word, signifies the human nature united to the Divine in the incarnation. These speculations are calculated to give very little satisfaction. How strange is it that none of these learned men have discovered that God himself interprets this name in <reference osisRef="Exo.34.6">Exo 34:6</reference>,! "And the Lord passed by before him, and proclaimed יהוה Yehovah the Lord God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty." These words contain the proper interpretation of the venerable and glorious name Jehovah. But it will be necessary to consider them in detail. <div eID="gen4031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4032" type="x-p"/> The different names in this and the following verse have been considered as so many attributes of the Divine nature. Commentators divide them into eleven, thus: - <div eID="gen4032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4033" type="x-p"/> 1. יהוה Jehovah. <div eID="gen4033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4034" type="x-p"/> 2. אל EL, the strong or mighty God. <div eID="gen4034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4035" type="x-p"/> 3. רחום Rachum, the merciful Being, who is full of tenderness and compassion. <div eID="gen4035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4036" type="x-p"/> 4. חנון Channun, the gracious One; he whose nature is goodness itself; the loving God. <div eID="gen4036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4037" type="x-p"/> 5. ארך אפים Erech Appayim, long-suffering; the Being who, because of his goodness and tenderness, is not easily irritated, but suffers long and is kind. <div eID="gen4037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4038" type="x-p"/> 6. רב Rab, the great or mighty One. <div eID="gen4038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4039" type="x-p"/> 7. חסד Chesed, the bountiful Being; he who is exuberant in his beneficence. <div eID="gen4039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4040" type="x-p"/> 8. אמת Emeth, the truth or true One; he alone who can neither deceive nor be deceived, who is the fountain of truth, and from whom all wisdom and knowledge must be derived. <div eID="gen4040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4041" type="x-p"/> 9. נצר חסד Notser Chesed, the preserver of bountifulness; he whose beneficence never ends, keeping mercy for thousands of generations, showing compassion and mercy while the world endures. <div eID="gen4041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4042" type="x-p"/> 10. נשא עון ופשע וחטאה Nose avon vaphesha vechattaah, he who bears away iniquity and transgression and sin: properly, the Redeemer, the Pardoner, the Forgiver; the Being whose prerogative alone it is to forgive sin and save the soul. ינקה(לו) נקה לא Nakkeh lo yenakkeh, the righteous Judge, who distributes justice with an impartial hand, with whom no innocent person can ever be condemned. <div eID="gen4042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4043" type="x-p"/> 11. פקד עון Poked avon, etc.; he who visits iniquity, who punishes transgressors, and from whose justice no sinner can escape. The God of retributive and vindictive justice. <div eID="gen4043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4044" type="x-p"/> These eleven attributes, as they have been termed, are all included in the name Jehovah, and are, as we have before seen, the proper interpretation of it; but the meaning of several of these words has been variously understood.
entries.d48a112deb024429da5767f368c8745607fbdb15: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen4044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4045" type="x-p"/> That will by no means clear the guilty - This last clause is rather difficult; literally translated it signifies, in clearing he will not clear. But the Samaritan, reading לו lo, to him, instead of the negative לא lo, not, renders the clause thus: With whom the innocent shall be innocent; i.e., an innocent or holy person shall never be treated as if he were a transgressor, by this just and holy God. The Arabic version has it, He justifies and is not justified; and the Septuagint is nearly as our English text, και ου καθαριει τον ενοχον, and he doth not purify the guilty. The Alexandrian copy of the Septuagint, edited by Dr. Grabe, has και τον ενοχον καθαρισμῳ ου καθαριει, and the guilty he will not cleanse with a purification-offering. The Coptic is to the same purpose. The Vulgate is a paraphrase: nullusque apud te per se innocens est, "and no person is innocent by or of himself before thee." This gives a sound theological sense, stating a great truth, That no man can make an atonement for his own sins, or purify his own heart; and that all have sinned and come short of the glory of God.
entries.7de8465a9ddf987a140b81a4487e31ed8fc20ae9: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen4045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4046" type="x-p"/> O Lord, let my Lord, I pray thee, go among us - The original is not יהוה Jehovah, but אדני Adonai in both these places, and seems to refer particularly to the Angel of the Covenant, the Messiah. See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Gen.15.8">Gen 15:8</reference>.
entries.d9963f68d1aa3ca307755e37bcb8a2f9a999db2c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen4046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4047" type="x-p"/> I will do marvels - This seems to refer to what God did in putting them in possession of the land of Canaan, causing the walls of Jericho to fall down; making the sun and moon to stand still, etc. And thus God made his covenant with them; binding himself to put them in possession of the promised land, and binding them to observe the precepts laid down in the following verses, from Exodus 34:11-26 inclusive.
entries.7683d9b701087072727282bab10d20786582b0de: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen4047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4048" type="x-p"/> Ye shall destroy their images - See the subjects of this and all the following verses, to <reference osisRef="Exo.34.28">Exo 34:28</reference>, treated at large in the notes on Exodus 23 (note).
entries.35a739ae0f9276f38cf3ce1e25dd917a6537c1d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen4048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4049" type="x-p"/> In earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest - This commandment is worthy of especial note; many break the Sabbath on the pretense of absolute necessity, because, if in harvest time the weather happens to be what is called bad, and the Sabbath day be fair and fine, they judge it perfectly lawful to employ that day in endeavoring to save the fruits of the field, and think that the goodness of the day beyond the preceding, is an indication from Providence that it should be thus employed. But is not the above command pointed directly against this? I have known this law often broken on this pretense, and have never been able to discover a single instance where the persons who acted thus succeeded one whit better than their more conscientious neighbors, who availed themselves of no such favorable circumstances, being determined to keep God's law, even to the prejudice of their secular interests; but no man ever yet ultimately suffered loss by a conscientious attachment to his duty to God. He who is willing and obedient, shall eat the good of the land; but God will ever distinguish those in his providence who respect his commandments.
entries.3a135d1d4c5c049f046279d2ac0e69dfe4b875e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen4049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4050" type="x-p"/> Neither shall any man desire thy land - What a manifest proof was this of the power and particular providence of God! How easy would it have been for the surrounding nations to have taken possession of the whole Israelitish land, with all their fenced cities, when there were none left to protect them but women and children! Was not this a standing proof of the Divine origin of their religion, and a barrier which no deistical mind could possibly surmount! Thrice every year did God work an especial miracle for the protection of his people; controlling even the very desires of their enemies, that they might not so much as meditate evil against them. They who have God for their protector have a sure refuge; and how true is the proverb, The path of duty is the way of safety! While these people went up to Jerusalem to keep the Lord's ordinances, he kept their families in peace, and their land in safety.
entries.b20bb7f56669e4444d279eb8345fe27a8e074940: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen4050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4051" type="x-p"/> The blood of my sacrifice - That is, the paschal lamb. See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Exo.23.18">Exo 23:18</reference> (note).
entries.a141fb47a77c2735c731ab7fbf76f0ad2128baf9: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen4051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4052" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk - See this amply considered <reference osisRef="Exo.23.19">Exo 23:19</reference> (note).
entries.54d4b6f931ec3a1b499ec3f1d5db6f52d0a72d14: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen4052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4053" type="x-p"/> Write thou these words - Either a transcript of the whole law now delivered, or the words included from <reference osisRef="Exo.34.11">Exo 34:11</reference> to <reference osisRef="Exo.34.26">Exo 34:26</reference>. God certainly wrote the ten words on both sets of tables. Moses either wrote a transcript of these and the accompanying precepts for the use of the people, or he wrote the precepts themselves in addition to the ten commandments which were written by the finger of God. See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Exo.34.1">Exo 34:1</reference> (note). Allowing this mode of interpretation, the accompanying precepts were, probably, what was written on the back side of the tables by Moses; the ten commandments, what were written on the front by the finger of Jehovah: for we must pay but little attention to the supposition of the rabbins, that the letters on each table were cut through the stone, so as to be legible on each side. See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Exo.32.15">Exo 32:15</reference> (note).
entries.2d68c90304501f5278fff884bf8e6a5048661d91: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen4053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4054" type="x-p"/> Forty days and forty nights - See Clarke's note on <reference osisRef="Exo.24.18">Exo 24:18</reference>.
entries.fa8c52eb14e89f1382dd1ff2d3811091cb8a76cc: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen4054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4055" type="x-p"/> The skin of his face shone - קרן karan, was horned: having been long in familiar intercourse with his Maker, his flesh, as well as his soul, was penetrated with the effulgence of the Divine glory, and his looks expressed the light and life which dwelt within. Probably Moses appeared now as he did when, in our Lord's transfiguration, he was seen with Elijah on the mount, Matthew 17. As the original word קרן karan signifies to shine out, to dart forth, as horns on the head of an animal, or rays of light reflected from a polished surface, we may suppose that the heavenly glory which filled the soul of this holy man darted out from his face in coruscations, in that manner in which light is generally represented. The Vulgate renders the passage, et ignorabat quod cornuta esset facies sua, "and he did not know that his face was horned;" which version, misunderstood, has induced painters in general to represent Moses with two very large horns, one proceeding from each temple. But we might naturally ask, while they were indulging themselves in such fancies, why only two horns? for it is very likely that there were hundreds of these radiations, proceeding at once from the face of Moses. It was no doubt from this very circumstance that almost all the nations of the world who have heard of this transaction, have agreed in representing those men to whom they attributed extraordinary sanctity, and whom they supposed to have had familiar intercourse with the Deity, with a lucid nimbus or glory round their heads.
